newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba may opt for 'double-decker' repo to help mark.
newsitem.headline: Buba may opt for 'double-decker' repo to help mark.

text.p: The Bundesbank could soon present financial markets with a nifty piece of footwork when it sets one of the most talked-about repurchase agreements in almost a year.

Speculation that the central bank will now have to act, and not just talk, to support the faltering mark has been heating up since last Thursday when the bank declined to set a repo rate for the whole of its four-week holiday period.

But with most sectors of the German economy only just starting to show a recovery, the Bundesbank must tread a fine line if any credit tightening is not to hamper growth and risk sending the economy back into recession.
"The Bundesbank would not want to see anything more than a 10 or 15 basis point rise in (money market) rates," said Jan Hatzius, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
"Certainly if we saw rates move up by 20 basis points, they would be uncomfortable."

In announcing fixed 3.0 percent repos for just two weeks last Thursday -- ahead of a four-week summer break -- the Bundesbank sparked talk that it was leaving its options open for the second half of the four-week holiday period.
Markets speculated that it could either tighten the rate, or allow market rates to drift up by setting a variable rate agreement.
But it could also do both.
Topping the list of possible moves being mooted in the markets is a so-called "parallel operation" combining both fixed and variable repo agreements.

With the fixed 3.0 percent rate, unchanged since last summer and now also set in place until August 12, markets may have to wait until then to find out what, if anything, Europe's most powerful central bank has up its sleeve.

But if the mark, which has stablised somewhat in recent session after hitting its lowest levels in more than seven years against the dollar, were to take another turn for the worse, the bank could also move on August 5 to add a variable repo to the already established fixed agreement.
"A parallel operation would be a way of sending a signal without really risking a major jump in money market rates," said Hatzius.
"I think it's quite possible that they will do that, but anything more drastic is less likely."

A parallel repo structure could, for example, incorporate a two-week fixed repo, under which banks are allocated funds at a fixed 3.0 percent cost, and a four-week variable tender under which banks bid for funds and rates float according to demand.

The structure would limit the scope for short rates to be pushed up and at the same time signal to financial markets that the Bundesbank does not want to see inflation threatened by a mark falling too far too fast.
Some analysts, however, said the Bundesbank could find that a double-decker repo would be a little too subtle.

"The risk for the Bundesbank is that it might take a much stronger rate increase to support the mark than the economy would be able to support," said Karl Haeling head of DMG futures and options in Frankfurt.

"And if the Bundesbank were to tip its hand with a modest but insufficient rate increase, it might then have spent its ammunition and have the worst of both worlds -- higher short rates and a weaker mark still pushing up import prices."

While it is no secret that import prices are seeing some upward pressure from the dollar -- June's data showed prices at their highest level for six years -- the direct impact of this on headline inflation so far has been limited. Import prices make up only around six percent of the Consumer Price Index basket.

Labour costs have been coming down this year, money supply growth is falling and reached the Bundesbank's target corridor last month, domestic demand is thin, economic growth is weak and consumer price inflation, while rising, is still comfortably below two percent.

Against that background, John Butler, senior fixed income analyst at WestLB in Duesseldorf, said that even the most delicate of moves in the form of a parallel repo operation was unlikely to materialise in the near term.

"I'm certain this is an idea that has been talked about at the Bundesbank as a way to marginally alter the monetary environment in Germany," he said. "But the real economy does not call for even a marginal rate increase at this time."

The Bundesbank may be eager to halt the mark's decline, he said, but not so eager as to risk the health of the German economy for the sake of what could be seen as merely a face-saving exercise in financial markets.
